column2: How many latent variables does a DDPM have, compared with a plain VAE?
column3: Many, \(x_1, \dots, x_T\) with \(T \approx 1000\), stacked in a chain, instead of one.

column2: What is the dimension of each DDPM latent \(x_t\)?
column3: The same as the data: \(\dim(x_t) = \dim(x_0)\). There is no bottleneck.

column2: Which half of a DDPM has learnable parameters?
column3: Only the reverse (decoding) direction. The forward (encoding) process is a fixed noising rule.

column2: In the diffusion literature, what do \(x_0\) and \(x_1, \dots, x_T\) denote?
column3: \(x_0\) is the clean data point. \(x_1 \dots x_T\) are the latent vectors obtained from it by progressive noising — not dataset indices, which is the notation an earlier essay in this series would have led you to expect.

column2: Why does the forward step use \(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\) and \(\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\) rather than \(\alpha_t\) and \(1-\alpha_t\)?
column3: So that variances add to one: if \(\mathrm{Var}(x_{t-1}) = 1\), then \(\mathrm{Var}(x_t) = \alpha_t + (1-\alpha_t) = 1\). The process is variance-preserving.

column2: Define the signal-to-noise ratio of \(x_t\).
column3: \(\mathrm{SNR}(t) = \bar{\alpha}_t/(1-\bar{\alpha}_t)\): signal variance over noise variance in \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon\).

column2: Under the standard linear schedule (\(T = 1000\)), roughly how much of \(x_0\)’s amplitude survives at \(t = T\)?
column3: About 0.6%: \(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_T} \approx 0.006\). Close enough to pure noise to start sampling from \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\).

column2: Why is \(q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})\) Gaussian, and what are its parameters?
column3: Because the forward step is \(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\) plus Gaussian noise, and adding a constant-scaled Gaussian keeps it Gaussian. The mean is \(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\) and the covariance is \((1-\alpha_t)I\).

column2: Derive, in outline, why \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\) has the closed form it does.
column3: Unroll the recursion: each substitution multiplies the previous signal by another \(\sqrt{\alpha}\) and adds independent Gaussian noise. A sum of independent Gaussians is Gaussian with added variances, so the accumulated signal coefficient is \(\sqrt{\prod_i \alpha_i} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\) and the accumulated noise variance is \(1 - \bar{\alpha}_t\).

column2: What is \(q(x_T)\) in the limit, and why does that matter for generation?
column3: With the schedule chosen so \(\bar{\alpha}_T \to 0\), \(x_T\) is essentially pure noise, distributed as \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\). That is the stationary distribution of the chain, and it is what makes generation possible: sampling can start from the prior, which you already know how to sample.

column2: What justifies writing \(P_\theta\) as a product of Gaussians?
column3: Nothing deeper than a modelling assumption: we choose the reverse process to be a first-order Markov chain with Gaussian transitions, and put neural networks on the means and covariances. The factorisation is a definition, not a theorem.

column2: In the DDPM reverse chain, what is \(P(x_T)\)?
column3: The fixed prior \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\), which is where sampling starts.

column2: Name the three terms of the DDPM objective.
column3: Reconstruction, \(\mathbb{E}_{q(x_1\mid x_0)}\log P_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\); prior matching, \(D_{KL}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\|P(x_T))\), which has no \(\theta\) and is dropped; and denoising matching over \(t = 2\dots T\), the only term that trains the network.

column2: Where does the telescoping happen, and what does it buy?
column3: Applying Bayes' rule to the forward conditional produces a \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)\) in the numerator and a \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\) in the denominator. Across the product over \(t\) every intermediate term cancels, leaving only \(q(x_1\mid x_0)\) and \(q(x_T\mid x_0)\). Those two ends are what become the reconstruction and prior-matching terms.

column2: Why can the prior-matching term \(D_{KL}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\|P(x_T))\) be dropped during training?
column3: Neither side contains \(\theta\): \(q\) is the fixed forward process and \(P(x_T)\) is the fixed prior. It is a constant.

column2: Why does the KL between these two Gaussians reduce to a squared error on the means?
column3: Because we set \(\Sigma_\theta = \Sigma_q\). The log-determinant ratio is zero and the trace of \(\Sigma_q^{-1}\Sigma_q\) is just the dimension, so both constant terms drop and only \((\mu_\theta-\mu_q)^T\Sigma_q^{-1}(\mu_\theta-\mu_q)\) survives — which for a scalar covariance is \(\|\mu_\theta-\mu_q\|_2^2\) up to the factor \(1/2\sigma_q^2\).

column2: Does the true reverse covariance \(\Sigma_q\) depend on the data?
column3: No. \(\Sigma_q = \frac{(1-\alpha_t)(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1})}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}I\) depends only on the schedule, which is why it is reasonable to fix \(\Sigma_\theta = \Sigma_q\).

column2: What is the network asked to predict, in this formulation?
column3: The mean of the reverse step, \(\mu_\theta(x_t)\). But since \(\mu_q\) is affine in \(x_0\) and \(\mu_\theta\) is forced to share that affine form with \(\hat{x}_\theta\) in place of \(x_0\), predicting the mean is equivalent to predicting the clean image \(x_0\) — hence a denoiser.

column2: What is the score of \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\) in terms of the added noise?
column3: \(\nabla_{x_t}\log q(x_t\mid x_0) = -\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\).

column2: A network trained by MSE to predict \(\epsilon\) from \(x_t\) learns what, at its optimum?
column3: The conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid x_t]\), because the MSE minimiser is always a conditional expectation.

column2: How do you turn a trained noise predictor \(\hat{\epsilon}_\theta\) into a score estimate?
column3: \(\nabla_{x_t}\log P(x_t) \approx -\hat{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t,t)/\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\) (Tweedie).

column2: Write the reverse-step mean \(\mu_\theta\) in terms of the predicted noise.
column3: \(\mu_\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t - \frac{1-\alpha_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}\hat{\epsilon}_\theta\right)\).

column2: Given \(x_t\) and a noise estimate \(\hat{\epsilon}\), what is the implied estimate of the clean image?
column3: \(\hat{x}_0 = (x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\hat{\epsilon})/\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\), by inverting the jump-to-any-time formula.

column2: What does the network see besides \(x_t\), and why is that necessary?
column3: The time step \(t\), encoded as a sinusoidal positional embedding. One network is shared across all noise levels, so without knowing \(t\) it could not tell a barely-noised image from one that is almost pure noise, and the optimal denoiser differs enormously between those cases.

column2: Why can training noise a single data point all the way to step \(t\) in one go?
column3: Because \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\) is Gaussian with known parameters, so \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon\) produces an exact sample from it. There is no need to simulate the intermediate steps during training, which is what makes each iteration cheap.

column2: Why is sampling a thousand times more expensive than one training step?
column3: Training needs one forward pass per iteration regardless of \(T\). Sampling needs a full pass at every step of the reverse chain, from \(t=T\) down to \(t=1\) — so \(T\) passes for a single generated sample. That asymmetry is precisely what DDIM later attacks.

column2: Write the "simple" noise-prediction loss that most DDPM implementations train on.
column3: \(\mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,\epsilon}\|\epsilon - \hat{\epsilon}_\theta(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon,\ t)\|^2\), with \(t\) uniform on \(\{1,\dots,T\}\).

column2: In DDPM sampling, what is different about the final step \(t = 1\)?
column3: No fresh noise is added: output \(\mu_\theta(x_1)\) directly as the clean sample.

column2: Where does the classifier's gradient come from in classifier guidance?
column3:
From Bayes' rule: \(
abla\log P(x_t\mid y) = 
abla\log P(x_t) + 
abla\log P(y\mid x_t)\), with the \(\log P(y)\) term dropping out. The diffusion model supplies \(
abla\log P(x_t)\) and a separately trained classifier supplies \(
abla\log P(y\mid x_t)\).

column2: What problem does classifier-free guidance solve, and at what extra cost?
column3: It removes the need for a separate classifier that must be robust at every noise level — instead one model is trained with the condition randomly dropped so it can also emit the unconditional score. The cost is two forward passes per sampling step instead of one.

column2: Write the classifier-free guided score in terms of conditional and unconditional scores and \(\lambda\).
column3:
\(	ilde{s} = 
abla\log P(x_t) + \lambda(
abla\log P(x_t\mid y) - 
abla\log P(x_t))\).

column2: In classifier-free guidance, what do \(\lambda = 0\), \(\lambda = 1\) and \(\lambda > 1\) give?
column3: \(0\): unconditional sampling. \(1\): the plain conditional. \(> 1\): extrapolation toward \(P(x_t)P(y\mid x_t)^\lambda\), sharper prompt-fidelity, less variety.

column2: How is one network trained to produce both conditional and unconditional scores?
column3: Randomly replace the condition with a null label \(\varnothing\) on a fraction of training examples (around 10%).

column2: What exactly does a latent diffusion model diffuse over, and who turns it back into pixels?
column3: It diffuses over the latent code \(z_0 = E_{\phi^*}(x_0)\) produced by a pretrained autoencoder. Generation samples \(z_{novel}\) by reverse diffusion and then applies the decoder, \(x_{novel} = D_{\theta^*}(z_{novel})\).

column2: Why is diffusing in an autoencoder’s latent space cheaper than in pixel space?
column3: The latent is much smaller and has discarded imperceptible detail, so each of the many network passes in sampling works on far fewer numbers.

column2: DDIM changes the forward process to be non-Markovian. Why does that not invalidate the trained network?
column3: Because the ELBO depends on \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\) alone, and the DDIM family keeps that conditional identical to DDPM's. The bound is the same, so the regression target is the same, so training a DDPM has implicitly trained every model in the family. Only the sampling procedure changes.

column2: What does setting \(\sigma_t = 0\) buy you?
column3: A deterministic reverse process: the only randomness is \(x_T\). Determinism gives two things — faster sampling, because the chain can be taken in large jumps rather than a thousand tiny ones, and unique invertibility, since a deterministic map can be run backwards to recover the noise for a given image.

column2: What are the three moves of one DDIM step?
column3: Estimate \(\hat{x}_0\) from \(x_t\) and \(\hat{\epsilon}\); re-noise it to the next level using \(\hat{\epsilon}\) as the noise direction; add fresh noise \(\sigma_t z\) (none when \(\sigma_t = 0\)).

column2: Write the deterministic (\(\sigma_t = 0\)) DDIM update.
column3: \(x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\,\hat{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\,\hat{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t)\), with \(\hat{x}_0 = (x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\hat{\epsilon}_\theta)/\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\).

column2: Why can DDIM skip steps (e.g. go from \(t\) to \(t - 50\))?
column3: Its update only needs \(\bar{\alpha}\) at the current and target level; nothing ties it to adjacent steps, and the training objective never assumed a step size.

column2: In the DDIM paper’s notation, what does \(\alpha_t\) denote?
column3: The cumulative product \(\prod_{i\le t}\alpha_i\) — what DDPM writes as \(\bar{\alpha}_t\). Mixing the two conventions is the commonest DDIM bug.

column2: An error \(\delta\) in a noise prediction becomes what error in the implied \(\hat{x}_0\)?
column3: \(\delta\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}/\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} = \delta/\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}(t)}\): huge at high noise, tiny at low noise. That is why \(x_0\)- and \(\epsilon\)-losses weight time steps differently.
